executive_summary: The defining thread running through today's content is the tension between institutional authority and political pressure, most sharply illustrated by the federal judge's decision to reopen the lawsuit linking Donald Trump and the IRS over the administration's so-called 'weaponization' fund. This ruling matters because it signals that the judiciary is actively asserting its role as a check on executive branch conduct, particularly where the use of powerful government institutions — tax enforcement, legal mechanisms, funding structures — intersects with partisan interests. Foreign Affairs reinforces this theme from a geopolitical angle, noting that Latin America is poised to become a strategic priority, a region where U.S. institutional credibility and foreign policy consistency will be tested precisely at a moment when domestic trust in those institutions is under judicial scrutiny. Together, these stories underscore a single, urgent question: whether American institutions — legal, executive, and diplomatic — can maintain their structural integrity under sustained political stress. The answer will have consequences far beyond Washington.

newsletters.title: Latin America Is About to Become a Priority

items.headline: Latin America Is About to Become a Priority for U.S. Foreign Policy
items.blurb: Trump Will Disrupt Three Decades of "Benign Neglect". A few weeks before Donald Trump began his second term, Brian Winter predicted that his presidency would "focus more attention on Latin America than any U.S. administration in perhaps 30 years." A year later, the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Today, the United States is putting immense pressure on Cuba, including by blocking its access to oil. Winter warned Latin American leaders, who for years had lamented a lack of attention from Washington, "Be careful what you wish for." He was right that Trump would turn to "tariffs, sanctions, and perhaps limited military action" to achieve his goals—but his essay is also a useful reminder that U.S.–Latin American relations could still change course, depending on whether Trump comes to see the region "as more of an opportunity than a threat."

items.headline: Two months in, two MLB teams tell the story
items.blurb: MLB's season crossed the two-month mark Thursday. Two teams, one in each league, explain the fun but odd vibe of the 2026 season to date: The Cubs are 31-27 with one of MLB's best lineups and five Gold Glove defenders, but their pitching staff has literally fallen apart. They have two winning streaks of 10 games but also just got off a 10-game losing streak Wednesday, making them the second team in league history — along with the 2017 Dodgers — to have three such streaks in a season. The Athletics are 27-30, have led their division for much of the year, and feature first baseman Nick Kurtz, a 23-year-old titan who's on a possible Hall of Fame track in his second season in the bigs.

items.headline: Another French Open stunner
items.blurb: Rather than dwell on how strange it is that a men's Grand Slam is about to be won by someone not named Carlos Alcaraz, Jannik Sinner or Novak Djokovic — all missing from the French Open's Round of 16 — let's take a beat to appreciate João Fonseca, who showed yesterday why some think he could reach that tier of tennis gods. The 19-year-old Brazilian was two sets down to Djokovic — previously 301-1 with a two-set lead — when he began his thrilling comeback, which The Athletic's Ava Wallace said was best exemplified by his well-roundedness in the 5-5 game of the fifth set.
